newsitem.title: UK: Oil price rise threatens British inflation goal.
newsitem.headline: Oil price rise threatens British inflation goal.

text.p: Spiralling oil prices will fuel UK inflation in the coming months, and could prove to be the final straw for the government's inflation target, economists said on Wednesday.
But they will have a limited impact on government finances as growing petroleum tax revenues may be offset by lower overall taxes as consumers feel the pinch, they added.

World oil prices have rocketed to five-year highs recently as tensions in the Middle East have conspired with diminished world stocks and rising winter demand to push crude values up 40 percent since June.

As a net exporter of oil, the impact on the UK economy is twofold. On the one hand, rising oil prices have already started to boost producer prices, sounding alarm bells for inflation, but on the other, rising prices for oil exports will bolster the UK's trade balance as much as 2.0 billion stg, economists say.
"If oil prices were to stay at current levels they would knock 1.5 to 2.0 billion stg off the trade deficit," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Ciaran Barr.
"The direct effect will be on the inflation side. If it all feeds through to the RPI it could go up 0.4," he said.
"But some of the rise will be absorbed and we don't think these high oil prices will be sustained, so maybe 0.2 will feed through to RPI."
Barr warned the oil price rise may prove to be the thorn in Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's side, preventing him from reaching his target of 2.5 percent core inflation by the end of the year.
"If inflation is struggling to fall to 2.5 percent, that could be the crunch that stops it getting there and could cause the Chancellor problems in the coming months," he said.
Core UK inflation edged up to 2.9 percent in September, stubbornly sticking to the upper half of the government's 1.0 to 4.0 percent target range.
Economists said sterling's unrelenting climb to a 21-month high versus the mark would help to choke some of the impending inflationary pressures, but not all.
Darren Winder at Warburgs said the impact on the economy would be modest. "The overall picture is that it is a relatively moderate impact unless oil prices go sharply higher from here," he said.
"The petroleum revenue tax accounts for relatively low revenues, so it will have a positive impact on the PSBR but the size of impact will be relatively small."
But James Capel economist David Bloom painted a much gloomier picture, saying the oil price rise would curb GDP growth and add to the government's debt burden.
"With the petroleum revenue tax, the government will get lots of extra money because a pound on the oil price is worth around 150 to 200 million stg in tax revenue," Bloom said.

"So although we'd get more on the petroleum side it's just not enough to overcome some of the losses you'd sustain on the public sector account through more sluggish growth, such as higher social security payments and lower tax revenues."

James Capel estimates that fixed exchange rates and an oil price of $25 a barrel, which the futures market is discounting for November, would reduce GDP growth by 0.1 percent in the first year and 0.3 percent in the second.
This in turn would add 0.9 percent and 0.7 percent to the retail price index with a net flat impact on the PSBR as a percentage of GDP in the first year and adding 0.7 percent to it in the second.
